raw:
The common room has settled into its second life by the time you pass through it. Cards snap against the low table by the fire. Dena, her splinted wrist resting carefully on a cushion, studies her hand with theatrical suspicion while Thessaly holds her own cards too upright to conceal anything.

“I understand the rules,” Thessaly says. “I dislike them.”

“You’ve played three hands,” Dena replies.

“That was enough.”

No one looks up for more than a moment as you continue to the library.

Its air smells of lamp oil, old bindings, and the faint mineral damp that clings to the Academy in storm weather. An iron spiral stair winds up through the center of the room. Open shelves rise on both levels, their sections marked in seven scripts; the nearby volumes concern treaty law, arbitration, Council proceedings, and commentaries dense enough to make the shelf sag.

Caelindra occupies one end of a long reading table beneath a green-shaded lamp. A stack of notes sits precisely squared at her elbow. She does not look up when you enter.

At the reference desk, an older human man in a dark, ink-marked coat is making notes in a ledger. He notices you studying the shelves and then the signet at your hand.

“You’re Rowan Garvey,” he says. “Gareth Stone. I teach human Covenant history.”

The organization turns out to be less helpful than it first appears: the Academy considers “introductory” material a subset of constitutional theory, while the most accessible-looking books are actually arguments about centuries-old tariff disputes. After a few minutes, you ask Stone for help.

He gets up without ceremony and leads you to a lower shelf near the desk. “Start here.”

He draws out a slim green volume with a worn gilt title: *The Council at Work: A Conclave Primer.*

“It covers the seven seats, committees, votes, arbitration, and the ways a treaty becomes binding. It will tell you what people mean when they use the phrases as if everyone was born knowing them.”

From the reading table, Caelindra turns a page.

“It calls the voting arrangement equitable,” she says. “Then puts the exceptions in a footnote forty pages later.”

Stone glances toward her. “Forty-one.”

“An improvement, then.”

He hands you the book. Its first page bears a neat Academy stamp and a list of former Conclave readers, none of the names familiar.

“Read the first three chapters,” Stone says. “After that, you’ll know enough to recognize when someone is explaining the Council to you selectively.”
